### 1. Introduction

Artificial intelligence (AI) has shifted from a specialised research topic to a pervasive, general‑purpose technology shaping daily life, economic systems, and public governance. It powers search engines, recommender systems, automated translation, fraud detection, logistics optimisation, and a growing range of public‑sector tools. As machine‑learning models have grown in scale and capability, societies have begun to ask more pointed questions about who benefits from AI, who bears the risks, and how it can be governed so that it advances human well‑being rather than undermining it.

“Responsible AI” is an umbrella term for the theory and practice of developing, deploying, and governing AI systems in ways that respect human rights, promote inclusion, protect the environment, and support equitable social and economic outcomes. Responsible AI is not a single law, standard, or checklist. It is a continuously evolving set of norms, institutions, and technical practices that must adapt to shifting capabilities, political contexts, and evidence about real‑world harms.

In recent years, governments have begun to codify principles of responsible AI into national strategies, sectoral regulations, and sometimes binding AI‑specific laws. International organisations have convened expert groups, drafted soft‑law instruments, and explored ways to align national approaches. Companies have established internal ethics boards, published model cards and system documentation, and experimented with new forms of assurance and auditing. Civil‑society organisations have documented abuses, raised the voices of affected communities, and proposed stronger safeguards.

Yet progress is uneven. Many countries lack the resources or institutional capacity to translate high‑level AI principles into enforceable rules. Others have adopted ambitious frameworks on paper but are still building the mechanisms to implement them. Some governments deploy AI for mass surveillance, social control, or discriminatory decision‑making, even as they present themselves as global leaders in responsible AI. Power asymmetries are stark: a handful of firms control much of the compute infrastructure and data that underpin cutting‑edge systems, while many countries remain reliant on imported technologies and models whose design and objectives they do not control.

Against this backdrop, comparative measurement becomes an important tool for understanding where the world stands on responsible AI. Rankings and indices cannot capture every nuance of governance, but they can help situate national efforts in a global context, highlight strengths and gaps, and inform public debate. The Global Index on Responsible AI (GIRAI), published by the Global Center on AI Governance, is one such effort. Now in its second edition (2026), GIRAI evaluates 135 countries across five dimensions—Inclusion and Diversity, Ethics and Sustainability, Labour and Skills, Trust and Safety, and AI Use in Public Service—mapped onto three pillars: AI Policy, Civil Society Organisation (CSO) Engagement, and Enabling Conditions.

GIRAI’s framework recognises that responsible AI is not only about what governments say, but also about what they do and how they are held to account. It therefore distinguishes between policy frameworks and concrete implementation initiatives, and it incorporates a penalty—URAI, or Unacceptable Risk AI—when there is documented evidence of government misuse of AI. The index draws on multiple evidence pathways, including formal national AI policy documents, government programmes, civil‑society initiatives, and documented cases of misuse.

This essay uses GIRAI’s lens to explore responsible AI in depth. It examines the principles underlying responsible AI, the global landscape of governance efforts, and the distribution of progress and gaps across regions and income groups. It considers inclusion and diversity, ethics and sustainability, labour and skills, trust and safety, and AI in public services as interconnected dimensions of a broader governance challenge. It also reflects on the roles of different actors—governments, companies, civil society, and international organisations—and on the tensions that arise when AI is used in environments marked by inequality, fragile institutions, or contested political power.

Responsible AI cannot be reduced to a technical problem, nor can it be addressed solely through national policy. It is a deeply political and social project that implicates questions of power, accountability, and global justice. The sections that follow unpack these themes, drawing on the GIRAI framework to illuminate where the world is making progress, where it is falling short, and what it might take to move towards a more equitable and human‑centred AI future.
